newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak doubts letter bombs came from Alexandria.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak doubts letter bombs came from Alexandria.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Tuesday he doubted letter bombs sent to London, Washington and New York came from Egypt, despite carrying Egyptian stamps and postmarks.

He told a news conference the Egyptian authorities had not received an original of the envelopes in which the letter bombs arrived, although 11 days have passed since the first of the letter bombs was detected in Washington.

An Egyptian government newspaper, quoting a senior security source, went further than Mubarak, saying it was impossible the 17 letters came from post offices in the Mediterranean city of Alexandria, the postmark they carried.

Mubarak said: "Really we have no definite answer for this. But I don't think that these letters are being sent from Alexandria. It's easy to imitate the stamps, to imitate everything (and) post them here and there."

"But we have very strict inspection on letters going abroad and even internally.... We are waiting to see a real letter coming from the States maybe today or tomorrow to make a complete check to know from where these letter bombs were sent," he said.
It was Mubarak's first comment on the letter bombs, which Interior Ministry officials and newspaper commentators have treated as an attempt to damage the country's image abroad.

In its report on Tuesday, the government newspaper al-Ahram said: "A senior security source confirmed...that the letter bombs sent to the offices of al-Hayat newspaper in London and Washington did not come from the Alexandria post office."

"The source said that extensive investigations undertaken by security authorities in the Interior Ministry, as well as search operations, revealed the impossibility that such letters came from Alexandria," the newspaper added.
The source said stamping postmarks on the envelopes after they were closed would make them explode immediately, so they could not have gone into the post through normal channels.
The U.S. embassy in Cairo has declined to give details of the investigation but legal attache Alfred Finch repeated on Tuesday that the U.S. and Egyptian authorities were cooperating.

No one has claimed reponsibility for the bombs, also sent to the U.N. bureau of the Saudi-owned al-Hayat, and the newspaper's journalists have speculated only that it may have made enemies by its coverage of the Middle East.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation has described as speculation a possible link with the Islamist groups which planted a bomb at the World Trade Center in New York in 1993 and planned to blow up the United Nations and other targets.

Three of the letter bombs turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas, which houses Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the World Trade Centre bombing, and Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh, who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters.
But a prominent Egyptian Islamist in exile, Yasser el-Sirri, told Reuters he did not believe Islamists did it, because they had no dispute with al-Hayat or the press in general.

In an unsolicited call from London, where he has political asylum, Sirri said he did not rule out the Egyptian authorities posting the letter bombs to pin the blame on Islamists, as part of the Egyptian campaign to persuade European countries to extradite Islamists in exile.
The al-Hayat office in Cairo now has police guards outside and journalists have instructions not to open letters from unknown sources, one of the journalists said.
But the staff did not feel they were a target because any letter bombs posted in Alexandria in late December should have reached them by now, said correspondent Mohamed Salah.
"Unfortunately in the Arab world we're not used to having a paper that is free and that reports the facts as they are without being coloured from governments or groups," he said.
